title: Sign This, Then Trust It: One Token Through ItsDangerous
premise: A web app wants to hand a user's identity — `{"id": 5, "name": "itsdangerous"}` — to an untrusted place (a URL, a cookie, an email link) and get it back later without a database lookup. The data must survive the round trip through hands that can read it and would happily edit it. ItsDangerous's answer is not encryption: the payload stays readable, but a keyed signature makes any edit detectable. This story follows that one dictionary out through `URLSafeSerializer.dumps` into the string `eyJpZCI6NSwibmFtZSI6Iml0c2Rhbmdlcm91cyJ9.6YP6T0BaO67XP--9UzTrmurXSmg`, and back in through `loads` — pausing wherever a default, a branch, or a comparison decides what the library actually guarantees.

chapters.title: Two Strings Become a Configuration
chapters.data_in: secret_key='secret key', salt='auth', and five Nones (serializer, serializer_kwargs, signer, signer_kwargs, fallback_signers)
chapters.data_out: A configured URLSafeSerializer: secret_keys=[b'secret key'], salt=b'auth', serializer=_CompactJSON, is_text_serializer=True, signer=Signer, signer_kwargs={}, fallback_signers=[]
facts: `_make_keys_list` normalises a single str/bytes key into a one-element list, so the key-rotation code path is the only code path — there is no special case for a single key.
Every textual input is funnelled through `want_bytes`, which UTF-8 encodes str and passes bytes through, so signing never depends on the caller's string type.

The salt is not a cryptographic salt in the password sense: it is stored as plain bytes and later concatenated into key derivation; the docs state it need not be secret or random, only unique per context.

`is_text_serializer` decides text-vs-binary by actually calling `serializer.dumps({})` at construction time and checking for `str` — a probe, not a declaration, and it runs the user-supplied serializer once during `__init__`.
`URLSafeSerializerMixin` overrides `default_serializer` to `_CompactJSON`, which sets `ensure_ascii=False` and `separators=(",", ":")`, so payloads are whitespace-free.
`fallback_signers` defaults to an empty list here: `Serializer.default_fallback_signers` is `[]`, and since 2.0 there is no implicit SHA-512 fallback.

open_questions.question: `is_text_serializer` came back True. What does that one boolean actually change about the token I hand out?
The single secret key was widened into a list. When does having more than one key in that list matter, and which one gets used?

chapters.title: A Dict Becomes a URL-Safe Payload
facts: The payload is encoded, not encrypted: `base64_decode` of the first token segment yields the original JSON, so anyone holding the token can read the id and name.
`Serializer.dump_payload` returns bytes unconditionally by passing the serializer's output through `want_bytes`, so a text serializer and a binary one converge here.

`URLSafeSerializerMixin.dump_payload` always calls `zlib.compress` and only keeps the result if `len(compressed) < len(json) - 1`; for this 30-byte JSON compression did not win, so the raw JSON was encoded — the compression cost is paid on every dump regardless.
When compression does win, a literal `b"."` is prepended as a marker — which is why the separator and the compression flag are both dots and why `unsign` splits from the right.
`base64_encode` uses `base64.urlsafe_b64encode` and strips `=` padding, which is what makes the payload safe in URLs and cookies.

open_questions.question: Nothing marks this payload as uncompressed. How will the reader on the other side know not to try `zlib.decompress`?

chapters.title: The Signer Is Built (and the Defaults It Carries)
chapters.data_in: salt=None → falls back to self.salt=b'auth'; secret_keys=[b'secret key']
chapters.data_out: A Signer with sep=b'.', salt=b'auth', key_derivation='django-concat', digest_method=_lazy_sha1, algorithm=HMACAlgorithm(_lazy_sha1)
facts: A fresh `Signer` is constructed per `dumps`/`loads` call rather than cached, so changing `secret_keys` or `salt` on the serializer takes effect immediately.
`make_signer` passes the whole `secret_keys` list to the signer, not just the newest key — the signer owns the rotation logic.

Road not taken: `Signer.__init__` rejects any separator that appears in `_base64_alphabet` (ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `=`) with a `ValueError`, because such a separator could occur inside the base64 signature and make splitting ambiguous. `b'.'` passes.

The default digest is SHA-1 via `_lazy_sha1`, which is deliberately a function rather than a direct `hashlib.sha1` reference so that importing the package does not fail on FIPS builds where SHA-1 is unavailable (CHANGES 2.2.0, issue 375).

SHA-1 as the HMAC inner hash is defended in docs/concepts.rst: collision weakness of the bare hash does not transfer to HMAC. A reviewer who disagrees can pass `signer_kwargs={'digest_method': hashlib.sha512}` plus a SHA-1 `fallback_signers` entry to migrate without invalidating old tokens.
Default key derivation is `django-concat`: `sha1(salt + b"signer" + secret_key)`. The docstring is explicit that this is not password stretching — the secret key must already be long and random.

open_questions.question: The separator `.` is also allowed to appear inside the payload segment. What stops a value containing a dot from confusing the reader?

chapters.title: Derive, HMAC, Append
facts: `derive_key()` with no argument uses `self.secret_keys[-1]` — the newest key signs, always.

The derived key here is `sha1(b'authsignersecret key').digest()` = `b'\xcea\x91\xbb...'`; the salt is therefore baked into the key, so a serializer with salt `upgrade` cannot verify a token signed with salt `activate`.
The signature is `HMAC(derived_key, payload, sha1)` base64url-encoded without padding: `6YP6T0BaO67XP--9UzTrmurXSmg`, 27 characters for a 20-byte SHA-1 digest.
The signature covers the base64 payload bytes exactly as they will appear in the token, not the original JSON or the original dict — so verification never has to re-serialize anything.
`sign` returns `value + sep + signature`; the payload is the prefix of the token in the clear.

Road not taken: `NoneAlgorithm` returns an empty signature and would produce a token with nothing after the dot — it exists for tests and for opting out of signing entirely, which defeats the library's purpose.

open_questions.question: The base64 signature had its `=` padding stripped. Will decoding it on the way back still work?

answers.answer: Because `is_text_serializer` was True, `dumps` ends with `rv.decode('utf-8')`, turning the signed bytes into the `str` the README prints. With a binary serializer (e.g. `pickle`) the same code returns raw bytes instead — the boolean decides the static and runtime type of everything `dumps` hands back.

chapters.title: The Token Comes Back from Outside
chapters.data_in: s='eyJpZCI6NSwibmFtZSI6Iml0c2Rhbmdlcm91cyJ9.6YP6T0BaO67XP--9UzTrmurXSmg' (a str from an untrusted caller), salt=None
chapters.data_out: b'...' bytes form of the token, plus a freshly built Signer (salt=b'auth') as the first and only candidate unsigner
facts: This is the trust boundary: everything from here on treats `s` as attacker-controlled. No parsing of the payload happens before the signature is checked.
`iter_unsigners` is a generator: it yields the primary signer first, then one signer per (fallback spec × secret key). With no fallbacks configured, the trace shows exactly one signer constructed.

Each fallback entry may be a dict of kwargs (reusing `self.signer`), a `Signer` subclass, or a `(class, kwargs)` tuple — the three shapes are distinguished by `isinstance` checks, so a fallback that is neither dict nor tuple is assumed to be a class.
`loads` swallows `BadSignature` per signer, keeps the last one, and re-raises it only after every candidate has failed — so a caller sees one exception, not the first failure.
Note the asymmetry: signing uses only the newest key, while `iter_unsigners` fans fallbacks across *all* `secret_keys`. Retiring a key means deleting it from the list.

Road not taken: `TimedSerializer.loads` is the same loop with one difference — `SignatureExpired` is re-raised immediately instead of being collected, because a correctly-signed-but-old token should not be retried against other signers.

open_questions.question: If every candidate signer rejects this token, what exactly does the caller get — and can they still see what the payload claimed to be?

chapters.title: Split, Decode, Compare in Constant Time
facts: `unsign` raises `BadSignature("No b'.' found in value")` before any splitting if the separator is absent — a token with no dot never reaches the crypto.
The split is `rsplit(sep, 1)`: only the last dot separates payload from signature, so dots inside the payload (including the zlib marker dot at the front) are harmless.

`verify_signature` wraps `base64_decode` in a bare `except Exception: return False` — malformed base64 in the signature is a plain verification failure, never a crash and never a distinguishable error.
`base64_decode` re-adds `=` padding with `b'=' * (-len(string) % 4)` and decodes with `errors='ignore'` on the ASCII step, which is why the padding-stripped signature round-trips.
The comparison is `hmac.compare_digest(sig, expected)` — a constant-time compare, so an attacker cannot binary-search a signature byte by byte from timing.

`verify_signature` iterates `reversed(self.secret_keys)`, trying the newest key first and falling back to older ones; here the loop matched on the first (only) key. Note the timing side channel this leaves is only *how many keys* were tried, not signature content.

On failure `unsign` raises `BadSignature(f"Signature {sig!r} does not match", payload=value)` — the rejected payload is deliberately attached to the exception for debugging, and `docs/serializer.rst` warns that decoding it is unsafe.

answers.answer: More than one key matters here: `verify_signature` loops over `reversed(self.secret_keys)` and accepts if any derived key matches, while `derive_key()` during signing takes `secret_keys[-1]`. That is the whole of key rotation — append a new key, drop the oldest, and tokens signed under either remain valid until the old key leaves the list.

`unsign` uses `rsplit(sep, 1)`, taking only the final dot as the boundary, and `Signer.__init__` guarantees the separator can never appear inside a base64 signature. So a dot in the payload — including the compression marker — cannot shift where the split lands.
Yes: `base64_decode` pads the string back to a multiple of four with `=` before calling `urlsafe_b64decode`, recovering the exact 20-byte digest `b'\xe9\x83\xfaO...'`.

They get the last `BadSignature` raised by `Serializer.loads`, carrying `payload=` the unverified value that was split off before the compare. `loads_unsafe`/`_loads_unsafe_impl` build on exactly that attribute, returning `(False, decoded_payload)` — useful for debugging, dangerous if the internal serializer is something like pickle.

chapters.title: Back to a Dict
chapters.data_out: {'id': 5, 'name': 'itsdangerous'} — equal to the dict that entered in chapter 2
facts: The decompression decision is made by a single sentinel check, `payload.startswith(b'.')` — the marker `dump_payload` prepends. This payload had no marker, so `zlib.decompress` was skipped entirely.

Deserialization happens only after verification in the normal `loads` path, so untrusted bytes never reach `serializer.loads` unless the HMAC matched — the key security invariant of the whole library.

Both decode steps convert arbitrary exceptions into `BadPayload` with `original_error` preserved: base64 failure, zlib failure, and JSON failure are all reported as bad payload rather than leaking the underlying exception type to the caller.

`BadPayload` is a `BadData` but *not* a `BadSignature`, so it escapes the `except BadSignature` loop in `loads` and propagates immediately — a valid signature over garbage is not retried against fallback signers.
Because `is_text_serializer` was True, `Serializer.load_payload` decodes the bytes as UTF-8 before handing them to `_CompactJSON.loads`; a binary serializer would receive the bytes directly.

Risk worth naming at sign-off: `zlib.decompress` runs on attacker-supplied bytes whenever the marker dot is present — but only after the signature check, so a decompression bomb requires the secret key. Anyone using `loads_unsafe` or `load_payload` directly on untrusted input loses that protection.

answers.answer: By the leading dot. `URLSafeSerializerMixin.dump_payload` prepends `b'.'` only when the compressed form was actually shorter; `load_payload` strips that byte and sets `decompress=True`. This payload started with `e`, so it was base64-decoded straight to `b'{"id":5,"name":"itsdangerous"}'` and parsed.
